messages.subject: latent mediator with continuous observed indicators and a binary outcome
messages.subject_clean: latent mediator with continuous observed indicators and a binary outcome
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yves et al.,

I have used lavaan to perform causal effects based mediation analysis for a single as well as multiple continuous mediators and a single binary outcome (and binary treatment/exposure). Thank you to Yves for sending me slides some time ago which pointed me to the paper by Muthen (2011) which then lead me to Muthen and Asparouhov (2014). Causal effects mediation modeling in SEM requires to write code beyond the SEM analysis (which provides the SEM parameter estimates) to compute the causal effects as "defined parameters" in the lavaan model specification. First it requires deriving the expectation of the outcome Y with exposure at value t and the mediator M at exposure t*, or E{Y(t,M(t*))}. For binary Y, this requires integrating the probability of Y conditional on M with respect to the distribution of M under t*. Muthen (2011) provides the mathematical details for this which helped me implement it in lavaan.

However, I now think that my data would be better fit by a continuous LATENT mediator with multiple observed (continuous) indicators. Muthen (2011) and Muthen and Asparouhov (2014) discuss latent mediators and their analysis in MPLUS, but do not provide any mathematical details/derivations about how E{Y(t,M(t*))} would now be derived or approximated (M is now the latent mediator). Now the models for outcome Y and the observed indicators all contain the latent mediator M, so it is not clear to me how to obtain E{Y(t,M(t*))}.
There are several papers (in particular Albert et al. 2016 Causal mediation analysis with a latent mediator) but they also do not seem to provide details on how to obtain E{Y(t,M(t*))} for binary Y and latent continuous M.

To summarize, I know how to do naive mediation analysis in lavaan with a binary outcome and continuous latent mediator with continuous observed indicators, but I am trying to figure out how to do the causal effects mediation analysis correctly.

Can someone help?
Thanks, Ina

Ina Hoeschele, Ph.D.
Professor, Fralin Life Sciences Institute at Virginia Tech,
Professor, Department of Statistics, Virginia Tech
Adjunct Professor, Wake Forest School of Medicine, Winston-Salem NC

I get an error rather than a warning, because the syntax you posted contains illegal model syntax:

> Y1~iy1(0.05)*1 #intercept for y1
> Y2~iy2(0.17)*1 #intercept for y2

Are you trying to simultaneously label and assign fixed values to those intercepts?

FYI, lavaan fixes the intercepts and variances of latent responses (assumed to underly ordered variables) by default, in order to identify the model.  If you are freeing those in your syntax, that is probably why your model is not identified.

messages.body_plain:
> How can I fix the error variance of 20% to this single indicator in syntax?

Are you saying the reliability of v9 is 0.8?  Then the ratio of the factor variance (psi3) to error variance (theta9) should be 0.8 / 0.2, and you can exploit this to specify a model constraint in your syntax:

Fac3 =~ 1*v9
Fac3 ~~ psi3*Fac3
v9 ~~ theta9*v9
## model constraint
theta9 == psi3 * 0.2 / 0.8 # implies theta9 / psi3 == 0.2 / 0.8

messages.subject_clean: Moderated Mediation-Probit link, computing conditional simple and indirect effects & plotting
messages.body_plain:
> When computing the indirect effect, what values is lavaan using to calculate the product of the indirect effect (a1*b1)

See your summary() output.  The parameter estimates with those labels are what lavaan multiplies, because that is what you told it to do.

> when a1 is an ML estimation and b1 is a probit link estimation?

I misspoke.  lavaan uses DWLS estimation, so they are both (weighted) least-squares estimates (but not ordinary/unweighted least squares).  If you set estimator="PML", you can get ML estimates of both.  The estimator applies to all parameters in the model, not each parameter separately.

> I am assuming that the unstandardized b and standardized B in the output for the ML estimate and the probit link estimates will be interpreted differently (e.g., a1 (ML): the mean of M changes for every unit change of the predictor; b1, direct and indirect effects (probit): the amount of z-score change in the outcome for every one unit change in the predictor)?

The interpretations (and link functions) do not depend on the estimator.  The (un)standardized estimates involving endogenous ordered variables are interpreted in terms of their latent response distributions, which are z-scores by default (parameterization="delta").  For binary outcomes, you can usually think of this as a latent propensity for being in the "higher" category.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> Is it safe to assume that the inclusion of predictors (all time-invariant) is the reason for the discrepancy?

Yes, the parameter estimates are covariances between residuals, so standardized estimates are partial correlations, not the zero-order (model-implied) correlations you get from lavInspect(fit. messages.body_plain:
> Is this what you meant when you said lavaan assigns fixed intercepts and variances to the latent responses?

Yes, delta parameterization fixes the total latent variances to 1, whereas theta parameterization fixes the residual latent variance to 1.  Either way, intercepts are fixed to zero by default.  Kamata & Bauer's (2008) excellent tutorial refers to these parameterizations as marginal and conditional, respectively.

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406

messages.body_plain:
> is it even possible to publish data with standardized path coefficient greater than 1.

Yes.  It is not a contradictory result.

> Or i received some artificial effect.

Did you receive a warning message about your variables having very different scales?  Looking at your residual variances, I would expect Zoo to have a much larger influence on the optimizer because its variance is so much larger.  The standardized slope > 1 has an exogenous predictor, so I cannot see anything about its scale.  Maybe try multiplying small-variance variables by 10 or dividing Zoo by 10 to get rid of the error, and see if it converges on a different solution.  Even if it does not, there is nothing necessarily wrong with these results.

> I know that a lot of people only looking on my results which immediately suggest that it is wrong.

You can refer reviewers to this post about how it is possible: https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/120201/magnitude-of-standardized-coefficients-beta-in-multiple-linear-regression

Hello,

I have a similar problem, though I have a regular 2 factor model (no crossloads), and I have 4 thresholds. What is the best way to obtain the CI's around a residual variance in that case?

On Monday, 18 November 2019 15:42:05 UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I end up with upper and lower CI values that are the same as the variance estimate, so it seems as if these are not quite right.
>
> No, that's right.  I didn't notice you had categorical outcomes, in which case the residual variances are not estimated by default.  There are a couple ways around this:
>

Hi Peter

On Mon, 10 Feb 2020 at 15:32, Peter MKUMBO <pmk...@g.clemson.edu> wrote:
> Thank you Jeremy for your response. I meant omnibus F-statistic for that particular "regression model" with nominal categorical predictors.
>

That's what I meant too. :)

Here's an example of what I was talking about.
set.seed(1234)

library(dplyr)

d <- data.frame(x = sample(1:5, 1000, TRUE))
d$y <- rnorm(1000) + d$x * 0.1

fit1 <- lm(y ~ factor(x), data = d)
summary(fit1)
anova(fit1)

d <- d %>%
  dplyr::mutate(x1 = x == 1,
                x2 = x == 2,
                x3 = x == 3,
                x4 = x == 4,
                x5 = x == 5)

library(lavaan)

model2 <- "
 y ~  x2 +  x3 + x4 + x5
 y ~~ y
 y ~ 1 "

fit2 <- lavaan::sem(model2, data = d)
summary(fit2)

model2a <- "
 y ~ b1 * x2 + b2 * x3 + b3 * x4 + b4 * x5
 y ~~ y
 b1 == 0
 b2 == 0
 b3 == 0
 b4 == 0"
fit2a <- lavaan::sem(model2a, data = d)
summary(fit2a)

The omnibus F test gives a p-value of 0.017. The parameter estimates in fit2 match the parameter estimates in fit1.

The fit2a chi-square test in the final model gives a p-value of 0.017, which is the same as the anova for fit1.

messages.body_plain:
> As you can see in the {sem} function above, I used "orthogonal=TRUE" and  "std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE" to make the factors orthogonal and to fix the variances of the factors to 1 (Reise, S. P., Moore, T. M., & Haviland, M. G., 2010). Is that correct?

 Yes, that is what those arguments do.  But note that for endogenous factors, you are setting the residual (not total) factor variance to 1.  It is just as arbitrary, and you can still find the standardized solution using summary(fit, std = TRUE) or standardizedSolution(fit)

> Even though I used "meanstructure = TRUE", the outputs of "Latent Variables" don't show 1 values for each of the defined latent factors. I assume this is because I used "std.ov = TRUE", but is that correct?

 I'm not sure why you expect mean structure parameters to be 1.  But you should not standardize your observed variables.  Doing so without placing appropriate constraints on residual variances makes your SEs and test statistics invalid.  Leave that out, and you can still obtain the standardized solution after the model is fit.

> Originally, I wanted to include four covarates as observed variables in the structural model specification, i.e., something like General2 ~ a*General1 + Gender + Ethnicity + age_mom_yr + Hamilton in the part of "# Structural model: Direct effect" above, but the model with this model specification did not converge and encountered error messages. Later, I found that people incorporate their covariates of interests as single-indicator latent variables, which is specified in the model above. Does this model specification make sense?? Here, the purpose of including those covariates is to see the effect of General1 on General2 after controlling for the covariates' effects on the variations of General2.

 That is what lavaan does already when you regress factors on observed variables.  To overcome convergence issues, you could consider setting conditional.x=TRUE, so that exogenous covariates are partialed out of modeled variables first, then the model is fitted to the residual covariance matrix.  This is computationally simpler, and might be advantageous.  However, it might be worth investigating why the convergence issues happen (e.g., multicollinearity?).

> If I want to approximate fit indices and their cut-points using the Bollen-Stine Bootstrapping Method, how can I incorporate it into this model? I've been struggling with this issue because I also used "missing = "fiml" to impute some missing values in the dataset.

FIML does not impute/replace missing values.  It simply utilizes all available information.  You can use bootstrapLRT() to obtain the Bollen-Stine p value for the chi-squared test, but you would have to program any model-based bootstrap of fit indices yourself.

messages.subject: Re: multilevel SEM with lavaan
messages.subject_clean: multilevel SEM with lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> Any idea what might be the problem?

lavaan does not yet fit ML-SEMs to categorical outcomes.  Although your binary variables are only the 3 predictors (right?), you are still telling lavaan to partition their variance into Level 1 and 2 components by modeling the binary predictors' effects at both levels.  That requires them to be random variables (i.e., fixed.x=FALSE).  I think you can only model them as fixed covariates by excluding them from the Level-2 model. See this example, adapted from ?Demo.twolevel

data(Demo.twolevel)
Demo.twolevel$g <- 1:0 # arbitrary binary variable
model <- '
    level: 1
        fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3
        fw ~ g
    level: 2
        fb =~ y1 + y2 + y3
        fb ~ g              # if you comment this out, the problem goes away
'
fit <- sem(model, data = Demo.twolevel, cluster = "cluster")
summary(fit)

But that would of course change the interpretation of the Level-2 coefficients because you would not be controlling for the same covariates.  If you are only interested in the Level-1 (within-subject) effects, you can just omit "level: 1" and "level: 2" from your model, and only specify a level-1 model in your syntax.  When you call lavaan with the cluster= argument, it will give you cluster-robust SEs and test statistics.

If you need to model both levels of analysis, you should just switch to fitting separate univariate MLMs for each mediator/outcome, then use the mediation package to calculate the (in)direct effects with robust CIs (they have good algorithms).  Find examples in their vignette:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mediation/vignettes/mediation.pdf

A limitation of both the cluster-robust single-level model AND a ML-SEM is the sphericity assumption, which is not necessarily tenable for repeated-measures data when they come from a longitudinal design (but it should be tenable if the repeated measures are experimental conditions whose order is counterbalanced across participants).  The only way (I can currently think of) around that limitation would be to switch the repeated measures to wide format and fit an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model, applying constraints to test whether effects remain constant over time (which is an assumption lavaan's ML-SEM would not allow you to test because it can only handle random intercepts).  But that is probably only feasible if you have relatively few repeated measures relative to your number of subjects.

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> I am confused that I don't see the variance of the indicator in your formula.

Not necessarily obvious, but they are equivalent.  Specifying the observed variance of the indicator allows you to explicitly set the constraint on the residual variance as a numeric value.  The formula above implicitly makes the same constraint, by constraining the ratio of psi / theta to be the ratio of reliability / unreliability.  A little algebra shows that this is equivalent to saying the total variance is equal to the sum of those 2 variance components.

The limitation of the implicit approach in this thread is that it relies on the model-implied rather than the observed indicator variance.  But with a single-indicator construct, I don't see a lot of room for such misspecification that would make the observed and model-implied indicator variance differ.

messages.subject_clean: fixed error variance for single indicator in CFA model with multiple and single indicators for constructs
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Is it possible to express your formula in the Mplus language?

Yes, you can use the NEW command to name the new variable, then define it below (I think in a MODEL CONSTRAINT command).  You can search for examples in the user guide or forum, especially in the mediation models, for defining new parameters.

> 2) On the Statmodel forum Linda said: "With categorical outcomes, residual variances are not parameters in the model.

Well, they are if you use parameterization = "theta", although they are nonetheless fixed (to 1) by default for identification.  But the issue with identification is that with a single continuous indicator, you only have 1 piece of observed information (the variance), so you can only estimate 1 piece of information (either the factor variance or loading, fixing the other to 1).  With a categorical indicator, you don't have an observed variance.  You are fitting the model to a polychoric correlation matrix, in which the (total) variances are fixed to 1.  So you cannot estimate anything in a single-indicator construct.

Using the default parameterization = "delta", the residual variances are fixed to 1 minus the common-factor variance for identification, such that the model-implied total variances == 1.  So the trick is simply to fix the factor loading to the square-root of the reliability, in which case the residual variance will be set to 1 minus the reliability.  For example, suppose the reliability of "u4" is 0.64 (however that is supposed to have been estimated...), the square-root of which is 0.8:

myData <- read.table("http://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap5/ex5.16.dat")
names(myData) <- c("u1","u2","u3","u4","u5","u6","x1","x2","x3","g")
model <- '
f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
f2 =~ 0.8*u4 # reliability == 0.64
'
summary(cfa(model, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:4), std.lv = TRUE))

Notice the the residual variance in the summary is fixed to 1 - 0.64 = 0.36

> But including a single indicator as a manifest variable (or as a latent with error fixed to 0, as lavaan does by default) would mean that we assume this indicator to be perfectly measured, right? Is it a valid assumption?  Kenneth Bollen, Les Hayduk and some other are clearly against this practice.

It's up to you.  I agree it is highly dubious to assume it is error-free, but it is also suspicious to use a reliability estimate for a single categorical item.  When we calculate scale reliability, it is the reliability of the composite (e.g., a scale sum or scale mean), not the reliability of each individual scale item.  If you are using a single categorical indicator, I doubt it is a composite of many items.  There is nothing wrong with choosing a few different values (including perfect reliability) and comparing results as a sensitivity analysis to different reliability assumptions.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I echo what Mauricio said about using a bootstrap CI for a significance test.  But I will note that the p value of an R-squared is obtained by a Wald test of the constraint(s) that all slopes predicting the outcome variable (e.g., latent intercept factor) are zero, which would imply R-squared == 0.  This is perfectly analogous to the omnibus F test in a regression model's ANOVA table, but it is an asymptotic chi-squared statistic instead.

>From the ?growth help page:

model.syntax <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
    s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4
  # regressions
    i ~ i_b1*x1 + i_b2*x2   # label your slopes
    s ~ s_b1*x1 + s_b2*x2
'
fit <- growth(model.syntax, data = Demo.growth)

lavTestWald(fit, constraints = ' i_b1 == 0 ; i_b2 == 0 ')
lavTestWald(fit, constraints = ' s_b1 == 0 ; s_b2 == 0 ')

messages.subject_clean: Imposing Correlation between endogenous variables
messages.body_plain:
> if I remember correctly you don't put the correlation between the variables themselves, but between their errors.

That is correct, but the lavaan syntax is written such that an endogenous variable's residual is identified using the name of the variable itself.

> > If you are familiar with Amos, you would have noticed that it is NOT possible to put a correlation "between two endogenous variable" OR "between an endogenous variable and an exogenous variable" .

Perhaps by default, but you should be allowed to estimate off-diagonal elements of the theta_epsilon matrix in Amos.  If Amos uses the full LISREL representation, in which case indicators of exogenous and endogenous factors are in different matrices, then that is the practical limitation that prevents correlating indicators of endogenous and exogenous factors.  But to be clear, all indicators are themselves endogenous (they are explained by the latent factors).

> > But this is not the exact case in R, lavaan. You can simply put correlation between two endogenous variable.

Correct.  And you can correlate any exogenous variables with the residuals of any endogenous variables.  This is because lavaan (like Mplus) uses only the "y side" of the LISREL representation.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Tue, Feb 11, 2020 at 12:19 PM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Any idea what might be the problem?
>
> lavaan does not yet fit ML-SEMs to categorical outcomes.  Although your binary variables are only the 3 predictors (right?), you are still telling lavaan to partition their variance into Level 1 and 2 components by modeling the binary predictors' effects at both levels.  That requires them to be random variables (i.e., fixed.x=FALSE).  I think you can only model them as fixed covariates by excluding them from the Level-2 model. See this example, adapted from ?Demo.twolevel
>
> data(Demo.twolevel)
> Demo.twolevel$g <- 1:0 # arbitrary binary variable
> model <- '
>     level: 1
>         fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3
>         fw ~ g
>     level: 2
>         fb =~ y1 + y2 + y3
>         fb ~ g              # if you comment this out, the problem goes away
> '
> fit <- sem(model, data = Demo.twolevel, cluster = "cluster")
> summary(fit)
>
> But that would of course change the interpretation of the Level-2 coefficients because you would not be controlling for the same covariates.  If you are only interested in the Level-1 (within-subject) effects, you can just omit "level: 1" and "level: 2" from your model, and only specify a level-1 model in your syntax.  When you call lavaan with the cluster= argument, it will give you cluster-robust SEs and test statistics.
>
> If you need to model both levels of analysis, you should just switch to fitting separate univariate MLMs for each mediator/outcome, then use the mediation package to calculate the (in)direct effects with robust CIs (they have good algorithms).  Find examples in their vignette:
>
> https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mediation/vignettes/mediation.pdf
>
> A limitation of both the cluster-robust single-level model AND a ML-SEM is the sphericity assumption, which is not necessarily tenable for repeated-measures data when they come from a longitudinal design (but it should be tenable if the repeated measures are experimental conditions whose order is counterbalanced across participants).  The only way (I can currently think of) around that limitation would be to switch the repeated measures to wide format and fit an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model, applying constraints to test whether effects remain constant over time (which is an assumption lavaan's ML-SEM would not allow you to test because it can only handle random intercepts).  But that is probably only feasible if you have relatively few repeated measures relative to your number of subjects.
>
> Good luck,
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Michelle,
  If you are unfamiliar with the concept of dummy coding, you can find a detailed presentation with examples in the regression/correlation text by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken.

  It is not clear why you think that it matters whether the categorical variable is time varying or not.

  Either way, you want to create two new variables such that they flag unique values of OG.  If you want to compare everyone to the OG = 2 group, then compute OG0 such that OG0 = 1 iff OG = 0, and otherwise OG0 = 0.  Likewise, compute OG1 such that OG1 = 1 iff OG = 1, and otherwise OG1 = 0.  You can check your work with contingency tables.  Everyone in the OG = 2 group should have both OG0 and OG1 equal to zero.  Remove OG from your model and replace it with OG0 and OG1 (or their counterparts if you choose a different reference group).  If OG were time varying, you would need to repeat this process for each OG variable.  Because it is time invariant, you should only have one OG variable and only need to do this once.

  The reason that it is okay to treat binary variable as numeric but not categorical variables with more than two values is that the key assumption is that all the intervals that are equal in numeric value are also equal in the differences that they represent.  Because binary variables have only two values, they have only one difference, and it has to be equal to itself.  However, as soon as you introduce three or more values, this no longer holds.  The difference between group 0 and group 1 may not equal the difference between group 1 and group 2.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

If you want to compare everyone to the OG = 2 group, then compute OG0 such that OG0 = 1 iff OG = 0, and otherwise OG0 = 0.  Likewise, compute OG1 such that OG1 = 1 iff OG = 1, and otherwise OG1 = 0.  You can check your work with contingency tables.  Everyone in the OG = 2 group should have both OG0 and OG1 equal to zero. messages.subject: Inconsistency in estimated covariance
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistency in estimated covariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a model where two LVs have just one indicator. My reasoning was that the covariance between them should be the same no matter whether they are just correlated factors in the model, or whether they are endogenous variables in a SEM. However, the covariance changes and I don't really understand why... I've put some example code below. I guess there's a specific reason for why lavaan behaves like this but I couldn't figure it out really...

Any help is appreciated. Pete

set.seed(123)

library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)

N <- 1000
Is <- rnorm(N, mean=5)

dat <- data.frame(x1 = Is * 0.35 + runif(N),
                  x2 = Is * 0.30 + runif(N),
                  x3 = Is * 0.25 + runif(N),
                  x4 = Is * 0.20 + runif(N),
                  x5 = Is * 0.15 + runif(N))

dat$y1 <- Is * 0.35 + runif(N)
dat$y2 <- Is * 0.25 + runif(N)

dat <- apply(dat, 2, scale)

round(cor(dat), 2)
# => correlation matrix between y1 and y2 = .51

# first model with correlated factors
str1 <- '
IV =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5
DV1 =~ 1*y1
DV2 =~ 1*y2
'
m1 <- sem(str1, data=dat, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, estimator="ML")
semPaths(m1, layout="tree2", whatLabel="est", intercepts=T, thresholds=T, residuals=T, exoCov=T, title=F, legend=F, mar=c(6,4,6,4))
summary(m1)
# => the covariance between DV1 and DV2 is .51 as in the correlation matrix shown above

round(cor(predict(m1)), 2)
# => the correlation between the predicted factor values for DV1 and DV2 is .51

# second model with some regressions (SEM)
str2 <- '
IV =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5
DV1 =~ 1*y1
DV2 =~ 1*y2
DV1 ~ IV
DV2 ~ IV
'
m2 <- sem(str2, data=dat, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, estimator="ML")
semPaths(m2, layout="tree2", whatLabel="est", intercepts=T, thresholds=T, residuals=T, exoCov=T, title=F, legend=F, mar=c(6,4,6,4))
summary(m2)
# => now the covariance between DV1 and DV2 dropped to .37. Why?

round(cor(predict(m2)), 2)
# => when I predict factor scores, the correlation between DV1 and DV2 is still .51...

# How can I get the correlation of .51 show as covariance between DV1 and DV2 (in model 2) when using a semPaths illustration?

messages.subject: Compare correlations between latent factors and observed variables
messages.subject_clean: Compare correlations between latent factors and observed variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan/semTools community,

I have a bifactor model with imputed data specified with 4 specific factors and a general factor for 3-level ordinal indicators. I have n=448 and data is missing for < 2% for any given indicator but for 14% with listwise deletion.
Like a lot of bifactor models it fits pretty well going by the conventional criteria. Looking at Omega H/Omega Total for factors, the general factor accounts for about 75% of reliable variance but one group factor accounts for a fair bit of the variance even after accounting for the general factor.

I want to examine correlations between latent factors and 7 observed variables (that are continuous but right skewed). I have questions about how do I go about doing this with lavaan syntax?

1. For specifying single indicator latent variable do I fix the indicator residual variance to zero like this?

Latent_Var = ~ Single_Var
Single_Var ~~ 0*Single_Var

2. If I specify correlations between the Latent_Var and all factors for the bifactor model, do i interpret returned estimates as bivariate correlations or are they partial correlations/something else? - I am estimating the model with std.lv <http://std.lv> = T. I find that if I specify all but one Latent_Var ~~ bifactor model factor correlation to 0 I can end up with the Latent_Var ~~ bifactor model factor estimate > 1.

3. Related to 2nd Question, if I include all observed variables in the model as single indicator latent variables, are the returned correlations between these single indicator latent variables bivariate or partial?

I guess these questions might be semnet related too but because I am using lavaan I thought I would try asking here first.

Thanks for your help,

Burt

messages.subject: Re: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
messages.subject_clean: How to interpret high P-value of Chi-square and RMSEA despite good CFI, SRMR and RMSEA values
messages.body_plain:
A non-significant p-value indicates good fit. So, if the other fit indices do as well this is consistent.

However, I do wonder about sensibility of estimating 37 parameters when n = 51 and that may be responsible for your error. I find it alarming to fit a model with so many parameters when your sample size is so small.

If you are fitting a regular CFA model I believe your code should be:

HS.model <- '
F1 =~ H2 + H3 + H5 + H6 + H9 + H12

F2 =~ H16 + H15 + H19 + H17 + H21 + H26
        '

It doesn't like you need a mean structure either. Try changing these and see if you still get a warning.

messages.body_plain:
Following Christopher
Ideally you have closer to 5 or more people for every variable, so your model is too complex for so few people. See Costello, A. B., & Osborne, J. W. (2005). Best practices in exploratory factor analysis: Four recommendations for getting the most from your analysis. Practical Assessment Research & Evaluation, 10(7), https://scholarworks.umass.edu/pare/vol10/iss11/17.

The warning message means no matter how well your model fits, it’s wrong. The covariance matrix is not positive definite. That usually means you have estimated too many factors for so few people. Usually you would need 12 items per factor to get a solution with only 50 people. See

Marsh, H. W., & Hau, K. T. (1999). Confirmatory factor analysis: Strategies for small sample sizes. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Statistical strategies for small sample research (pp. 251-284). London: SAGE Publications.

Marsh, H. W., Hau, K.-T., Balla, J. R., & Grayson, D. (1998). Is more ever too much? The number of indicators per factor in confirmatory factor analysis. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 33(2), 181-220. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr3302_1

messages.subject: Confidence intervals for CFI and RMSEA difference
messages.subject_clean: Confidence intervals for CFI and RMSEA difference
messages.body_plain:
I came across a very interesting paper on model comparisons:

Lai, K. (2019). Confidence Interval for RMSEA or CFI Difference Between Nonnested Models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 27(1), 16–32. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1631704

Here's the abstract:

In addition to evaluating a single model, often one also uses RMSEA and CFI to compare the
fit of multiple candidate models. Model selection based on ΔRMSEA and ΔCFI can be
meaningful because (a) showing a model is better than another is more scientific and easier
than showing a model is “good;” (b) it avoids the problems with cutoffs for fit indices; (c)
one is less likely to overlook other equally substantively plausible models. However,
currently, such model selection is based on sample ΔRMSEA and sample ΔCFI, which
can be much smaller, much larger, or even of opposite sign than the population values.
Accordingly, we propose analytic confidence intervals for population ΔRMSEA and ΔCFI.
The methods are applicable to both nonnested and nested models, robust to nonnormal data,
computationally efficient, and do not assume any candidate model is true. Simulation studies
verified our proposed methods are trustworthy

To me, this approach seems very promising. Is the suggestion by Lai something that could be implemented in semTools? Please see the paper for further details. The important parts are sections with technical details, but the paper also has awell-written introduction on problems in relying on cuttoffs for fit indices.

Christopher Bratt

messages.subject: Bifactor latent mean difference
messages.subject_clean: Bifactor latent mean difference
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues

Let us say that we have a model with nine indicators (assumed continuous) that is modelled as a bifactor model with three group factors (so all items load on the general factor and one respective group factor). I am interested in the latent mean score difference on the general factor for a binary group. Would it suffice to use the group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts") with std.lv <http://std.lv> = T to get the standardized mean score difference? I tried the measEQ.syntax in semTools and it warned me:

 "a factor's mean cannot be freed unless it has at least one indicator without a cross-loading whose intercept is constrained to equality".

The model syntax for group means sets the two latent means of GEN to 0:

## LATENT MEANS/INTERCEPTS:

A ~ c(alpha.1.g1, alpha.1.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
B ~ c(alpha.2.g1, alpha.2.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
C ~ c(alpha.3.g1, alpha.3.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
GEN ~ c(alpha.4.g1, alpha.4.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1

Is it then possible to examine latent mean score differences of the general factor in the bifactor model, and if so, must the group factor means for A, B, C be set to (0, 0) or could it be (0, NA) instead?

Thank you very much.

On Tuesday, February 11, 2020 at 7:28:31 AM UTC-5, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > How do I now run the indirect effects to test mediation?
>
> The same way you would in any other context.  Use the ":=" operator to specify the indirect effects of interest.  I assume you made equality constraints on AR and CL paths by using the same labels for multiple parameters. Those are the labels you use to define your indirect effects.
>
> > A few of my A->B, B->C paths are significant, so I need to run several indirect effect paths.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean.  Equality constraints mean that (direct effect) parameters are equal over time.  By implication, any indirect effect is also equal over time, assuming it is constructed from direct effects that are equal over time.
>

Hi Mauricio,

My bad! I completely understand now. Thank you so much for your clarification.

1. So I would need to first create dummy code variables

diss$OG1 <- car::recode(dat$OG, "0=0;1=1;2=0")
diss$OG2 <- car::recode(dat$OG, "0=0;1=0;2=1")

2. then run the model

model <- '
  # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    i =~ 1*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 1*JD3
    s =~ 0*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 2*JD3

    i ~ OG1*OG2 # control for OG1 and OG2
    s ~ OG1*OG2

'
fit <- growth(model, data = diss)

Just one more question, if I want to control for OG variable, which became OG1 and OG2, should I multiply those or add those in the model?
I multiplied them in the symtax I provided, but wasn't completely sure.
Thank you so much again for your help!

Best,

>
> Michelle
>
> No, if OG has 3 categories, you cannt just include as that. In that way it will be treated as continuous.
>
> You have to either create 2 dummy code variables, or do the model as multiple group for each category of OG

>

I was confused by grouping them into two categories as OG has 3 categories.
> >
> > I just wanted to confirm that below script is correct to control for OG while you examine changes in JD?

> > model <- '
> >   # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
> >     i =~ 1*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 1*JD3
> >     s =~ 0*JD1 + 1*JD2 + 2*JD3
> >
> >     i ~ OG # control for time invariant covariate
> >     s ~ OG

> > On Sunday, February 16, 2020 at 7:03:35 PM UTC-6, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal wrote:
> > > What Keith said
> > >
> > > I will only add the R code example on how to create these dummy variables
> > >
> > > Assuming the data frame is called "dat", and we are using group 0 as the reference group
> > >
> > > ###
> > > dat$OG1 <- car::recode(dat$OG, "0=0;1=1;2=0")
> > > dat$OG2 <- car::recode(dat$OG, "0=0;1=0;2=1")
> > >
> > >
> > > On Saturday, February 15, 2020 at 9:59:30 AM UTC-6, Nickname wrote:
> > > > Michelle,
> > > >   If you are unfamiliar with the concept of dummy coding, you can find a detailed presentation with examples in the regression/correlation text by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken.
> > > >
> > > >   It is not clear why you think that it matters whether the categorical variable is time varying or not.
> > > >
> > > >   Either way, you want to create two new variables such that they flag unique values of OG.  If you want to compare everyone to the OG = 2 group, then compute OG0 such that OG0 = 1 iff OG = 0, and otherwise OG0 = 0.  Likewise, compute OG1 such that OG1 = 1 iff OG = 1, and otherwise OG1 = 0.  You can check your work with contingency tables.  Everyone in the OG = 2 group should have both OG0 and OG1 equal to zero.  Remove OG from your model and replace it with OG0 and OG1 (or their counterparts if you choose a different reference group).  If OG were time varying, you would need to repeat this process for each OG variable.  Because it is time invariant, you should only have one OG variable and only need to do this once.
> > > >
> > > >   The reason that it is okay to treat binary variable as numeric but not categorical variables with more than two values is that the key assumption is that all the intervals that are equal in numeric value are also equal in the differences that they represent.  Because binary variables have only two values, they have only one difference, and it has to be equal to itself.  However, as soon as you introduce three or more values, this no longer holds.  The difference between group 0 and group 1 may not equal the difference between group 1 and group 2.

> Is it then possible to examine latent mean score differences of the general factor in the bifactor model

It is possible, but arbitrary.  Because the means of your observed variables are each influenced by the means of 2 latent variables, there is not enough information in the data to distinguish between differences due to the general factor and differences due to the specific factor.

> must the group factor means for A, B, C be set to (0, 0) or could it be (0, NA) instead?

That would arbitrarily identify your model, so you could estimate the group-2 general-factor mean (difference).  But that would only be valid if the specific-factor means do not differ between groups, which you cannot verify.  The possibility of finding a solution provides no protection against the potential (and likely) invalidity of that solution.

Michelle,
Two additional comments on your question:

First, bear in mind that the Lavaan model specification syntax is its own syntax distinct from model formulae used elsewhere in R.  That is why, for instance, the asterisk can mean something different in each.

Second, dummy codes have the unusual property of structural zeros because the values are mutually exclusive.  In your case, you have three groups, and four combinations of values on the two dummy codes.  As such, one such combination remains unused.  If you code the dummy variables as flags for a given value, then you have group 1 (1,0), group 2 (0,1), and group 3 (0,0).  However, you have no cases with the combination 1,1.  As a consequence, if you were to compute an interaction term as the product, it would be a constant, always equal to zero.  Alternatively, if you had coded group 3 as 1,1, then the product term would be a group 3 indicator, which is redundant because a case is in group 3 iff it is not in either group 1 or group 2.  Basically, your two dummy variables encode everything that there is to know about your three-valued variable.  There is no further information for a product term to encode.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Burt,
  I have to wonder if there is not a deeper quandary behind your question.  The fundamental equation in SEM is Sigma^ = Sigma(theta) meaning that the implied moments are those implied by the model given parameter values as arguments.  The idea is that the parameters on the right-hand side explain the moments, such as correlations, on the left-hand side.

  It seems as if you are trying to put a correlation or covariance on the right-hand side as a parameter.  This can be done for convenience in simple cases, but it is generally not explanatory to place correlations or covariances on the right-hand side (in the model).  These are often interpreted as shorthand conveniences for implicit latent variables with affects on both the variables involved in the residual covariance.

  If you are just interested in the correlations, you can obtain these using lavInspect() and choosing what='cor.all'.  This will give you model-implied correlations between all variables, latent and observed.

  If you are looking for a substantive interpretation of parameters, it may help to think of the residual/disturbance/uniqueness for a variable in the model as a separate latent variable with its own substantive interpretation.  One way to think of it is as a linear bundle of the omitted determinants of the value for that variable.  You can then interpret the correlation or covariance between the residual and any other variable as an association with that bundle (rather than as a correlation with the variable as whose residual that bundle serves).

  In terms of lavaan syntax, in a sense x ~~ y means something different depending upon whether either x or y is an endogenous variable.  You can obtain a unified interpretation but not by trying to assimilate the endogenous case to the case where both are exogenous.  Instead, think of the exogenous case as a special case in which the residual variable happens to be coextensive with the exogenous variable to which it is attached (because there are no other causal variables).  Understood that way, x ~~ y always refers to a correlation between latent variables representing the residuals of x and of y.

  I could be missing something but I hope that helps.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Michelle,
Thresholds and intercepts are distinct parameters in the model, not two words for the same thing.  If you have not already, I strongly recommend some introductory reading on categorical data in SEM.  There is a lot to be aware of and it is not something you want to try to pick up on the fly.  A good SEM text is helpful to have at hand when toubleshooting an analysis.

You are working with a complex model.  For learning purposes, I would suggest that you first practice with simpler models, such as a growth curve with continuous variables, a path model with ordinal indicators, before trying to put all the elements together into one model.  That way, you can better isolate problems and see how things work in with fewer moving parts.

A very good strategy is to first write out the model you want to fit (or draw it with all parameters labeled).  Then write the syntax.  Then use the lavaanify() function to view the resulting parameter table.  Finally, check the table against your model to match up all the parameters.  If you prefer to see the parameters in their matrices, use lavInspect() with what='free'.  It is helpful to compare this to a parameter table at least once.

When you declare a variable as ordinal, at least two things happen.  First, the model is augmented to include a new latent continuous variable specific to that observed variable and a threshold model that relates the observed variable to the latent continuous variable through a set of cut points at which the continuous variable is broken into categories (just one threshold for dichotomous variables).  Second, the estimation procedure changes from something like maximum likelihood to something like diagonally weighted least squares.

Exogenous variables do not need to be declared ordinal because the rest of the model can be estimated conditional upon exogenous variables, and they are thus free of the normality assumption required for maximum-likelihood type estimators.  Endogenous variables need to be declared ordinal because they will violate this assumption.  Diagonally weighted least square is a computationally less intensive cousin of asymptotically distribution free estimation that allows you to estimate the parameters without the normality assumption when using thresholds for ordinal variables.  This comes at the cost of larger sample size requirements.

The assumption of equal intervals has more to do with the interpretation of the effect parameters in linear models.  The slope tells you how much y is expected to change for any unit change in x.  This is a single values assumed to hold for all values of x (e.g., a change from 1 to 2 as well as a change from 2 to 3).  This constancy of effect is implausible if the change from 1 to 2 does not represent the same amount of change in x as the change from 2 to 3.  Dummy coding essentially lets you estimate separate slopes for different pairs of values of x.

Finally, if you are not doing so already, consider using the simulateData() function to simulate your data from a model expressed in lavaan syntax.  If you do that, it forces you to specify every parameter in syntax.  You can then work backwards by removing some of the specified values to create model syntax for fitting the model with some parameters set free.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Please find a related question and response from Mauricio:

Hi Mauricio,

I have estimated a single factor CFA model in Lavaan, and I derived factor scores using LavPredict. My dataframe, however, contains missing data, and it does not appear that LavPredict is able to calculate SEs for each estimated factor score when observations are not complete. I attempted to use your suggested blavaan code below, setting save.lvs=T, but I receive a similar error:

blavaan ERROR: lvs cannot currently be saved when data are missing.

Do you have any suggestions to work around this limitation and calculate SEs of the factor scores?

Thanks,
Adam

Adam

This is an issue with the new default Stan parameterization. If you want to extract factor scores you can use the old Stan method (target="stanclassic"), which the only disadvantage is that is slower. With missing data the posterior log-likelihhod will be slower, either way. I am showing an example at the end

Now, in general, it is not recommended to use factor scores as this does adds factor inderterminancy issues. Some, can be solve by treating factor scores from posterior draws as multiple imputations to account for factor indeterminancy and sample variability. This can be done with the function plausibleValues from semTools, which does work with blavaan objects

Please continue these questions in the blavaan google group forum. This way more people can help, and it stays there so other users can search for similar issues

Hope this helps

library(blavaan)
future::plan("multiprocess")
library(simsem)

## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'

dat_test <- imposeMissing(HolzingerSwineford1939,
                          pmMCAR=.2)
summary(dat_test)

fit <- bcfa(HS.model, std.lv <http://std.lv/>=T,
            save.lvs=T, target="stanclassic",
           data = dat_test)
summary(fit, standardized=T)

lvs <- blavInspect(fit, "lvmeans")
head(lvs)
> >

messages.body_plain:
> Instead of using dummy variable, is there any other method to deal the exogenous variable which is having more than two categories? My direct question is, Can I get one path coefficient for above stated simple example?

What coefficient do you want to interpret?  Would you like to assume that the difference in latent education level (i.e., the normally distributed variable assumed to underlie the outcome's ordinal categories) is the same between "poor" and "middle" wealth as it is between "middle" and "rich" wealth?  To model a single linear effect under such an assumption, merely code the categories with equidistant numbers like (0, 1, 2) or (1, 2, 3), then enter that numeric variable as the predictor of education level.

But you can test whether that assumption is tenable by treating "middle" as the reference category (i.e., using dummy codes for "poor" and "rich" as the 2 predictors of education level).  You can label their slopes (which are both mean differences compared to "middle"), then define a parameter that is the difference between those slopes.  The summary() output will give you a z test of the null hypothesis that those mean differences are equal.  If it is significant, you can reject the null hypothesis of a single linear effect.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> FIML is not imputation.  It merely uses all available information per case to estimate parameters.

> > I was wondering whether the syntax to test this models looks correct according to you?
>
> You mean the indirect and total effects?  Yes, the parameter labels are consistent with a textbook 3-variable mediation model.
>
> >
> > When I had a look at the fit indices, I got some ‘strange’ results (“perfect” fit indices) e.g., CFI = 1, RMSEA = 0 and Chi squared = 0. And I’m not sure whether this suggest that I did something incorrectly, or whether these values of the fit indices are plausible?
>
> You only have 3 variables, and you estimate the relationship between each pair, so your model is saturated (df = 0).  Fit will be arbitrarily perfect.  All you can do is interpret and test individual parameters.
>
> >
> > My final question concerns the 95% CI of the parameter estimate of the indirect effect. I inspect these CIs my models to evaluate the significance of the indirect effects. However, I am not sure which type of CIs LAVAAN generates by default (bias-corrected CI, or another type?)?
>
> By default, they are percentile intervals, but you can change that.  Read the ?parameterEstimates help page.
>

> On Feb 22, 2020, at 8:47 AM, 'Nickname' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Michelle,
> Thresholds and intercepts are distinct parameters in the model, not two words for the same thing.  If you have not already, I strongly recommend some introductory reading on categorical data in SEM.  There is a lot to be aware of and it is not something you want to try to pick up on the fly.  A good SEM text is helpful to have at hand when toubleshooting an analysis.
>
> You are working with a complex model.  For learning purposes, I would suggest that you first practice with simpler models, such as a growth curve with continuous variables, a path model with ordinal indicators, before trying to put all the elements together into one model.  That way, you can better isolate problems and see how things work in with fewer moving parts.
>
> A very good strategy is to first write out the model you want to fit (or draw it with all parameters labeled).  Then write the syntax.  Then use the lavaanify() function to view the resulting parameter table.  Finally, check the table against your model to match up all the parameters.  If you prefer to see the parameters in their matrices, use lavInspect() with what='free'.  It is helpful to compare this to a parameter table at least once.
>
> When you declare a variable as ordinal, at least two things happen.  First, the model is augmented to include a new latent continuous variable specific to that observed variable and a threshold model that relates the observed variable to the latent continuous variable through a set of cut points at which the continuous variable is broken into categories (just one threshold for dichotomous variables).  Second, the estimation procedure changes from something like maximum likelihood to something like diagonally weighted least squares.
>
> Exogenous variables do not need to be declared ordinal because the rest of the model can be estimated conditional upon exogenous variables, and they are thus free of the normality assumption required for maximum-likelihood type estimators.  Endogenous variables need to be declared ordinal because they will violate this assumption.  Diagonally weighted least square is a computationally less intensive cousin of asymptotically distribution free estimation that allows you to estimate the parameters without the normality assumption when using thresholds for ordinal variables.  This comes at the cost of larger sample size requirements.
>
> The assumption of equal intervals has more to do with the interpretation of the effect parameters in linear models.  The slope tells you how much y is expected to change for any unit change in x.  This is a single values assumed to hold for all values of x (e.g., a change from 1 to 2 as well as a change from 2 to 3).  This constancy of effect is implausible if the change from 1 to 2 does not represent the same amount of change in x as the change from 2 to 3.  Dummy coding essentially lets you estimate separate slopes for different pairs of values of x.
>
> Finally, if you are not doing so already, consider using the simulateData() function to simulate your data from a model expressed in lavaan syntax.  If you do that, it forces you to specify every parameter in syntax.  You can then work backwards by removing some of the specified values to create model syntax for fitting the model with some parameters set free.
>
> Keith
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.

messages.subject: Re: How do we visualize the conceptual map for publish purpose?
messages.subject_clean: How do we visualize the conceptual map for publish purpose?
messages.body_plain:
Harry,
  The resource that Carl suggested is great.  I might note, however, that while I am not sure what the difference is, I use plain vanilla Dia.  I have never heard of Dia Portable.

  It might be helpful to take a step back and look at the relationship between concept maps, causal diagrams, and path diagrams.  Concept maps are the most general class because the links between nodes differ in type and are explicitly labeled by type in the diagram.  Moreover, the reference of the nodes is determined contextually because different kinds of relations apply to different kinds of things.  These are not widely used in reporting SEM results.

  Causal diagrams and path diagrams are two distinct representations of causal relationships.  Causal diagrams are more abstract than path diagrams in that they represent a causal structure rather than a specific statistical model.  The provide a minimally sufficient representation to facilitate investigating certain causal and probabilistic relationships based on the structure.  These can be used to present theory, but are generally insufficient to adequately report a SEM analysis.

  Path diagrams represent SEM models.  It is a rule of path diagrams that every parameter estimated in the model is visually represented in the diagram.  Path diagrams are designed to provide sufficient information for someone to read the equations in the model from the diagram.  Generally, this is the kind of diagram that you want to use to report analysis or your results.  This is why your question elicited an answer about path diagrams.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Multilevel Sample Moments
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel Sample Moments
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

lavInspect(object, "sampstat") gives the observed sample statistics, it includes the 'ordinary' covariances that cov2cor() will transform into 'ordinary' Pearson correlations in a single-level model.

In a two-level model, sampstat gives the upper and the lower covariance, then I also apply cov2cor() to get correlations.

But the values are not the same as the ones provided by the function statsBy from the R package ‘psych’, a main purpose of statsBy is: "Perhaps the most useful part of statsBy is that it decomposes the observed correlations between variables into two parts: the within group and the between group correlation."

And psych manual adds "This follows the decomposition of an observed correlation... …discussed by Pedazur (1997) and by Bliese in the multilevel package."

It seems there are at least to ways to decompose the observed correlation. I would appreciate if somebody could confirm it.

And if so, could I get a reference of the procedure in lavaan (as package ‘psych’ prints Pedazur and Bliese in the manual)? A published paper (using lavaan) specifying the reference of the multilevel sample moments would be equivalent.

Please, note this is not about Implied moments of the model. Just sample moments in multilevel (decomposition of observed correlations).

Thank you very much in advance for your help!

Xavier Suriol

Syntax in lavaan:

lavInspect(<two-level fit object>, "sampstat")

cov2cor(lavInspect(object, "sampstat")[[1]][[1]]) # to get the lower level correlation

cov2cor(lavInspect(object, "sampstat")[[2]][[1]]) # to get the upper level correlation

Syntax in psych:

library(psych)

multilevelPsych <- statsBy(Dataset[c(<variables>,"SelfCode")],group="SelfCode")

multilevelPsych$rwg # correlation in the lower level

multilevelPsych$rbg # correlation in the upper level

messages.subject: Questions about using lavaan with multiple imputations on longitudinal data with multiple groups
messages.subject_clean: Questions about using lavaan with multiple imputations on longitudinal data with multiple groups
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we are trying to fit a CFA model with several latent factors measured by ordinal indicators in two time points and between two groups of participants. We have had some success with specifying and running smaller models (for individual constructs), but run into some issues when putting them all together. We have several questions, some theoretical, some practical:

1) Since we are using ordinal indicators, we are using the WLSMW estimator. We have found in the literature that this requires a sample size between 200 and 500. But how does this work with multigroups structure? Does it mean that we would need 500 participants per group?

2) Some pooled estimates have infinite degrees of freedom, is this a problem, and what does it mean? How can p vales even be calculated with infinite degrees of freedom?

3) How exactly are standardized solutions pooled across imputations? In our case factor loadings, for example, have the same values for standardized and non-standardized parameter estimates. This is not the case when evaluating models on individual imputed datasets.

4) Pooled outputs have fit indices in two columns, what is the difference between the two? The values reported by anova() correspond to the left column.

5) Our more complex measurement models (6 constructs, 2-5 indicators each) have some problems in estimating fit using the mi.cfa() function. Even though the model converged for the vast majority of imputations, we can't get a pooled estimate of model fit. We can get the coefficients if calling summary() with fit.measures=FALSE argument, but every time we try to acces the model fit we get the following error: Error in calculate.D2(w, DF, asymptotic = TRUE) : (list) object cannot be coerced to type 'double'

6) Finally, we would like to test the invariances using the measEq.syntax() function to produce model descriptions. However, the documentation for this function is very scarce, is there some literature somebody can point us to when using this function? How do we access the model descriptions for various models generated by the function? Does this function test the models against each-other, how does it choose which parameter estimates to show. It says in the documentation "Optionally returns the fitted model (if data are provided) representing some chosen level of measurement equivalence/invariance across groups and/or repeated measures", but what does chosen mean here, how do we choose?

Thank you very much for your time,

Blaž

messages.subject: Re: Questions about using lavaan with multiple imputations on longitudinal data with multiple groups
messages.subject_clean: Questions about using lavaan with multiple imputations on longitudinal data with multiple groups
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Since we are using ordinal indicators, we are using the WLSMW estimator. We have found in the literature that this requires a sample size between 200 and 500. But how does this work with multigroups structure? Does it mean that we would need 500 participants per group?

For asymptotic behaviors to kick in, yes, but the N required also depends on the size of your model and reliability of your indicators.  Models that estimate more parameters (which are closer to zero in the population) require more data for stability.

> 2) Some pooled estimates have infinite degrees of freedom, is this a problem, and what does it mean? How can p vales even be calculated with infinite degrees of freedom?

A t distribution with infinite df is the normal distribution.  The semTools package just rounds df > 9999 to Inf to prevent ugly displays (and because there is no practical difference between t and z statistics.

> 3) How exactly are standardized solutions pooled across imputations?

The same way as for complete data, but using pooled unstandardized estimates, which are standardized using pooled saturated-model estimates.

> In our case factor loadings, for example, have the same values for standardized and non-standardized parameter estimates. This is not the case when evaluating models on individual imputed datasets.

Really?  If you are using parameterization="delta" and std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, you should expect them to be the same because they are by definition.  If you think something is amiss, please provide a reproducible example.

> 4) Pooled outputs have fit indices in two columns, what is the difference between the two? The values reported by anova() correspond to the left column.

As with complete data, the second column contains robust test statistics.  I am working on synchronizing the print methods with lavaan before the next version goes to CRAN.

> 5) Our more complex measurement models (6 constructs, 2-5 indicators each) have some problems in estimating fit using the mi.cfa() function. Even though the model converged for the vast majority of imputations, we can't get a pooled estimate of model fit. We can get the coefficients if calling summary() with fit.measures=FALSE argument, but every time we try to acces the model fit we get the following error: Error in calculate.D2(w, DF, asymptotic = TRUE) : (list) object cannot be coerced to type 'double'

Are you using the latest development version?

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

If so, please provide a reproducible example (syntax and enough data to generate the error, so I can track down the issue).

> 6) Finally, we would like to test the invariances using the measEq.syntax() function to produce model descriptions. However, the documentation for this function is very scarce, is there some literature somebody can point us to when using this function?

That's probably the most detailed help-page I have written, other than permuteMeasEq(), but I do agree a vignette is in order.  Here is a problematic tutorial that I do not find very accurate:  https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1602776

I am planning to write a better one after I make it though some major life events.

> How do we access the model descriptions for various models generated by the function?

What is a "model description"?  Have you used the summary() or as.character() methods, as shown in the help-page examples?  What specific information would you like to access?

> Does this function test the models against each-other, how does it choose which parameter estimates to show.

Again, see the help-page examples to illuminate how to use the function.

> It says in the documentation "Optionally returns the fitted model (if data are provided) representing some chosen level of measurement equivalence/invariance across groups and/or repeated measures", but what does chosen mean here, how do we choose?

Using the group.equal= and long.equal= arguments.  But as the help page says, I do not recommend automatically fitting the model.  I recommend inspecting the syntax that the function writes, to verify you are fitting the model you intend to fit (or to learn how to specify the model using certain guidelines, controlled by the ID.* arguments).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: [simsem] two group latent change score model power analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan and simsem developers/maintainers,

first of all, I want to thank you for the brilliant packages!

I know lavaan quite well but I'm only starting to work with simsem. I want to use the latter to determine the necessary sample size for a forthcoming study where I will estimate latent change score models in a control group and an experimental group. My approach follows ex24 from the simsem wiki.
I define a nested model where the intercept of the change factor is zero and a parent model where that intercept is freely estimated at a certain value. I want to identify which combinations of effect size and sample size will allow me to detect significant differences between the models.

My code (with strict measurement invariance across time points) produces the following error message:
Error in lambda %*% totalFactorCov : non-conformable arguments

Can anyone please give me a hint where the error in my code is?

Thank you very much in advance!

Best
Luc

library(simsem)

### NESTED MODEL

# factor loadings
loading <- matrix(0, 6, 2)
loading[1, 1] <- "l1"
loading[2:3, 1] <- c("l2", "l3")
loading[4, 2] <- "l1"
loading[5:6, 2] <- c("l2", "l3")
LY <- bind(loading, "runif(1, 0.5, 0.8)")
LY

# factor variances
VE <- bind(c(1, 0, 1))
VE

# factor correlations
facCor <- matrix(NA, 3, 3)
diag(facCor) <- 1
facCorVal <- diag(3)
facCorVal[1, 2] <- facCorVal[2, 1] <- "runif(1, 0.7, 0.95)" # pre~post
facCorVal[2, 3] <- facCorVal[3, 2] <- "runif(1, 0.4, 0.7)" # lc~post
facCorVal[1, 3] <- facCorVal[3, 1] <- "runif(1, -0.2, 0.2)" # LC~~Pre
RPS <- binds(facCor, facCorVal)
RPS

# mean structure
ALnested <- bind(c(0, 0, 0))
ALnested

# equal intercepts
inter <- rep(NA, 6)
inter[1] <- inter[4] <- "int1"
inter[2] <- inter[5] <- "int2"
inter[3] <- inter[6] <- "int3"
TY <- bind(inter, 1)
TY

# residual variances across time
resvar <- rep(NA, 6)
resvar[1] <- resvar[4] <- "res1"
resvar[2] <- resvar[5] <- "res2"
resvar[3] <- resvar[6] <- "res3"
VTE <- bind(resvar, "runif(1, 0.4, 0.6)")
VTE

# residual covariances across time
error <- diag(6)
error[1, 4] <- error[4, 1] <- "res1"
error[2, 5] <- error[5, 2] <- "res2"
error[3, 6] <- error[6, 3] <- "res3"
errorVal <- diag(6)
errorVal[1, 4] <- errorVal[4, 1] <- "runif(1, 0.4, 0.6)"
errorVal[2, 5] <- errorVal[5, 2] <- "runif(1, 0.4, 0.6)"
errorVal[3, 6] <- errorVal[6, 3] <- "runif(1, 0.4, 0.6)"
RTE <- binds(error, errorVal)
RTE

# generate nested model
lcsmNested <- model(LY = LY,
                    RPS = RPS,
                    VE = VE,
                    AL = ALnested,
                    TY = TY,
                    VTE = VTE,
                    RTE = RTE,
                    modelType = "CFA")

### PARENT MODEL

# mean structure
ALparent <- bind(c(0, 0, "runif(1, 0.8, 1.2)"))
ALparent

# generate parent model
lcsmParent <- model(LY = LY,
                    RPS = RPS,
                    VE = VE,
                    AL = ALparent,
                    TY = TY,
                    VTE = VTE,
                    RTE = RTE,
                    modelType = "CFA")

# fit nested and parent model on data from nested model
outDatNestedModNested <- sim(1000, n = 200, lcsmNested, generate = lcsmNested)
outDatNestedModParent <- sim(1000, n = 200, lcsmParent, generate = lcsmNested)

anova(outDatNestedModNested, outDatNestedModParent)

Hi all, I am still quite new to SEM (especially anything more complex than a CFA) and I have been trying two different identification approaches for my factor-of-curves model.

- All variables are continuous. ["tot", despite its name, is not a sum of the other two variables or anything of the sort, it's just another continuous variable.]
- N = 1084, but I have various missing data at various time points, so I'm using the   missing = "ML"   argument

The first model I specified is the following:
model1 <- '
#growth curves
Imat =~ 1*mat_w1 + 1*mat_w2 + 1*mat_w3 + 1*mat_w4
Smat =~ 0*mat_w1 + 2.96*mat_w2 + 6.71*mat_w3 + 9.8*mat_w4

Iblk =~ 1*blk_w1 + 1*blk_w2 + 1*blk_w3 + 1*blk_w4
Sblk=~ 0*blk_w1 + 2.96*blk_w2 + 6.71*blk_w3 + 9.8*blk_w4

Itot =~ 1*tot_w1 + 1*tot_w2 + 1*tot_w3 + 1*tot_w4
Stot=~ 0*tot_w1 + 2.96*tot_w2 + 6.71*tot_w3 + 9.8*tot_w4

#domain parameters
Iv =~ NA*Imat + Iblk + Itot
Sv =~ NA*Smat + Sblk + Stot

#lv as scaling reference: var=1, int=0
Iv ~~ 1*Iv
Sv ~~ 1*Sv
Iv ~ 0*1
Sv ~ 0*1

#estimate covariances between lv for each task
Imat ~~ Smat
Iblk~~ Sblk
Itot ~~ Stot
'
fit1 <- growth(model1,dset1, missing = "ML")

This simply throws the warning: "lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative", but otherwise works fine. The negative variances (Smat and Stot) are not significantly different from 0 and model fit indices are good or very good. Fixing those two variances at 0 makes the warning disappear and doesn't really affect fit indices

This is the alternative model
model2 <- '
#growth curves
Imat =~ 1*mat_w1 + 1*mat_w2 + 1*mat_w3 + 1*mat_w4
Smat =~ 0*mat_w1 + 2.96*mat_w2 + 6.71*mat_w3 + 9.8*mat_w4

Iblk =~ 1*blk_w1 + 1*blk_w2 + 1*blk_w3 + 1*blk_w4
Sblk=~ 0*blk_w1 + 2.96*blk_w2 + 6.71*blk_w3 + 9.8*blk_w4

Itot =~ 1*tot_w1 + 1*tot_w2 + 1*tot_w3 + 1*tot_w4
Stot=~ 0*tot_w1 + 2.96*tot_w2 + 6.71*tot_w3 + 9.8*tot_w4

#domain parameters (first indicator load = 1 by growth default)
Iv =~ Imat + Iblk + Itot
Sv =~ Smat + Sblk + Stot

#lv as scaling reference for the mean: int=0
Iv ~ 0*1
Sv ~ 0*1

#estimate covariances between lv for each task
Imat ~~ Smat
Iblk~~ Sblk
Itot ~~ Stot
'
fit2 <- growth(model2, dset1, missing = "ML")

However, in this case I get "lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!", and consequently no St. Error estimation and no fit indices for my model.

Finally, if I use what I learned from model1 about negative lv variances and define model2.1 accordingly:
model2.1 <- '
#growth curves
Imat =~ 1*mat_w1 + 1*mat_w2 + 1*mat_w3 + 1*mat_w4
Smat =~ 0*mat_w1 + 2.96*mat_w2 + 6.71*mat_w3 + 9.8*mat_w4

Iblk =~ 1*blk_w1 + 1*blk_w2 + 1*blk_w3 + 1*blk_w4
Sblk=~ 0*blk_w1 + 2.96*blk_w2 + 6.71*blk_w3 + 9.8*blk_w4

Itot =~ 1*tot_w1 + 1*tot_w2 + 1*tot_w3 + 1*tot_w4
Stot=~ 0*tot_w1 + 2.96*tot_w2 + 6.71*tot_w3 + 9.8*tot_w4

#domain parameters (first indicator load = 1 by growth default)
Iv =~ Imat + Iblk + Itot
Sv =~ Smat + Sblk + Stot

#lv as scaling reference for the mean: int=0
Iv ~ 0*1
Sv ~ 0*1

#estimate covariances between lv for each task (not for var = 0)
# Imat ~~ Smat
Iblk~~ Sblk
# Itot ~~ Stot

#fix negative lv variances at 0
Stot ~~ 0*Stot
Smat ~~ 0*Smat
'
fit2.1 <- growth(model2.1, dset1,  missing = "ML")

At this point, model2.1 works fine, converges and gives results equivalent to those of model1

QUESTIONS
1) If those two "negative" variances are the problem, why does model 1 work at least somewhat fine, and model 2 completely fail to converge?
2) What kind of information should I try to extract from model 2 in order to identify the problem (Seeing as it's not throwing a nice, detailed, informative warning as model 1 did)?
    I tried with lavInspect(fit2, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>") and something is clearly off, but I wouldn't have been able to look at this and know how to fix it, if I hadn't run model 1 beforehand

> > Imat  1.000
> > Smat -0.162  1.000
> > Iblk  0.765  0.001  1.000
> > Sblk   0.000 -0.004 -0.174  1.000
> > Itot  0.635  0.001  0.637  0.000  1.000
> > Stot    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN  1.000
> > Iv      0.873  0.001  0.876  0.000  0.727    NaN  1.000
> > Sv        NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN    NaN  1.000

2.1) Does a correlation matrix like the above mean that Stot and Sv probably have a negative variance? (also, note so far it has been Smat, and not Sv, to have an estimated negative variance)

I guess what I'm trying to ask is: in the future, if I find myself in a "model 2" situation, how do I identify the problem? Do I have to try and specify the model in another way, or is there something else to look at?

3) I know I still make basic mistakes and fail to notice them, so maybe the issue comes from somewhere else entirely?

Thanks for any kind of help
Federica

messages.body_plain:
Federica,
  This kind of issue received a lot of attention for simpler SEM models in the early days of SEM.  Here are some general strategies.

1. Try using previous research to choose better start values.
2. Try fitting the model from a variety of different start values (this was automated in Mx).
3. Try extending the number of iterations, or refitting the model using the non-converged estimates as start values.
4. Try fitting a simplified model to obtain reasonable start values for some of the parameters and then use those to fit the full model.
5. Try to intuit potential problems from unusual or out-of-bounds values among the non-converged parameter estimates.

  It may be that in fitting simplified submodels, you would also discover parameters such as yours that can be fixed to zero.  Negative variances are nonsensical, and thus always indicate a problem somewhere in the model.  Nothing can vary less than a constant.

Keith
